entries.title: The DNC Put Up Its Headquarters as Collateral to Obtain Its Massive Loan
entries.summary: It’s raised concern among members that it’s further evidence of the financial strain the committee is under.
entries.content:
The Democratic National Committee put its physical headquarters up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15 million line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, according to D.C. deed records not previously reported.

The building, located in Southeast Washington and partially owned by the DNC, has been used as collateral in the past, including in other election cycles. That the DNC had to do so again ahead of the 2026 elections to obtain its biggest-ever off-year loan raised concerns among some members that it was further evidence of its intensifying financial strain.

The DNC did not explicitly declare the building as its collateral in its monthly or loan-related filings to the Federal Election Commission.

“Ken gaslighting us about the DNC’s finances and not being transparent about the financial situation makes us doubt if he can oversee the DNC during the most important primary of our lifetime,” said a DNC member, granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly.

The DNC is working toward two main goals: to help the party win back control of Congress in November, as well as gubernatorial and local elections across the country. And it’s also preparing for the 2028 presidential primary, which is expected to be wide open and have no clear front-runner.

Those objectives have been complicated by the DNC’s current lack of money. Federal disclosures from June showed it only had about $16 million in its account and $18 million in debt. That’s a sobering amount of money compared to the Republican National Committee, which declared that it had $128 million in cash with no outstanding debts.

"This is not new,” said a DNC official in a statement about the party using the building as collateral. “The loan documents were publicly released in November, and the DNC's building was also used as collateral in our prior lines of credit in 2019, 2018, 2014, and many other years."

Another Democrat close to the DNC said Ken Martin, the beleaguered Democratic Party chair, has struggled to convince donors to maximize their contributions, which has contributed to the small cash-on-hand total.

Martin is under particularly close scrutiny. He was the subject of an internal human resources inquiry after throwing a phone in the direction of a young aide in early July, according to five sources who have direct knowledge of the situation or were briefed on the matter. The New York Times first reported the phone-throwing incident.

It’s the latest internal flare-up for the chair, who is tasked with reversing the party’s fortunes but faces growing skepticism amid paltry fundraising numbers and a botched release of the 2024 election autopsy that almost cost him his position as chair. For some of those sources, the incident with the cellphone reflected a tense mood inside the DNC that has only deepened.

The incident occurred after call time, a block in his schedule where Martin would call political allies or donors. While the details of what set Martin off are unclear, multiple people who were briefed on the matter said he got angry and threw his phone in the direction of his aide, though it did not hit the staffer. The incident left a small group of aides who were present shaken and resulted in a human resources inquiry, two of the five sources said.

It is unclear who placed the HR inquiry.

“It’s just fucking unnacceptable. This is spiraling behavior,” said one DNC source briefed on the incident.

Another source who heard about it said it was “not surprising,” given Martin’s recent demeanor.

Another source who was familiar with the incident said the phone was thrown at the aide’s desk and not at the aide, which they argued made the incident less severe.

All of the sources who spoke to NOTUS requested anonymity for fear of retaliation.

Martin, who was elected as DNC chair in February of 2025, apologized to the aide the following business day in a meeting with HR, a DNC source said, and the committee has tried to move past this incident. NOTUS is declining to name the aide involved.

The aide did not respond to a request for comment from NOTUS.

Martin in the meantime has been on the defensive about the DNC publicly. Last week, he defended the committee’s current financial status as a new strategy in an op-ed on Substack. Responding to criticism of the party’s low cash-on-hand totals, Martin wrote that the DNC has made the “conscious decision” to invest the cash it raises into “electoral assets: more people, earlier organizing, better technology, and stronger state parties.”

“That answer may be unsatisfying to people who believe the purpose of a political party is to accumulate the largest possible bank balance until the final days before an election,” Martin said. “But a party is not a savings account. Its purpose is to build power.”

Martin also wrote that the DNC has “done exceptionally better with high-net worth donors,” citing an increase of donations from major donors relative to comparable years.

The DNC is also grappling with fallout from the changes it wants to make ahead of 2028. On Friday, its rules committee approved a new 2028 Democratic presidential calendar — but not before serious sparring among states that wanted to be in the early window. The voting schedule, which has South Carolina voting first, followed by Nevada and New Hampshire, still needs to go before the full DNC for a vote in its August meeting, but already at least two states have made their displeasure at the order public.

The pressure of the job, three Democrats close to the DNC told NOTUS, appears to be having an effect on Martin. One of the three sources pointed to the controversy Martin faced over the incomplete 2024 election autopsy in May as the inflection point.

NOTUS reported a brewing crisis over Martin’s leadership after the autopsy. It was released with errors and ultimately failed to reach an explanation for what went wrong. It also failed to include an executive summary, even though one was mentioned in the report. The blowback grew contentious — sources NOTUS spoke to at the time said that Martin refusing to share the larger problem of the autopsy with a broader group of officials at the DNC contributed to the outsized reaction. There was even talk of a no confidence vote, though it never came to pass.

“He’s been super paranoid,” said one of the DNC sources of Martin’s recent behavior. “He’s super embattled.”

That source pointed to the fact that DNC officers were asked to sign nondisclosure agreements in advance of a meeting concerning its financial circumstances as an example. The nondisclosure agreements were first reported by Axios and confirmed by NOTUS.

“He’s not in a great place at all,” said one of the sources close to Martin. “I’m very concerned.”
entries.author: Elena Schneider, Jasmine Wright

entries.title: What the Nationals' First Deadline Deal Really Means
entries.summary: The Nats traded infielder Curtis Mead to the Red Sox on Saturday in exchange for pitcher Connelly Early.
entries.content:
In late March, the Nationals traded a young catcher named Boston Smith for an Australian infielder named Curtis Mead, who had been solidly below-average in 488 career plate appearances — and was just designated for assignment by the White Sox, a team that lost 102 games in 2025. And then late Saturday night, the Nats flipped Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early, which was both their first trade deadline deal and a clear self-assessment for the new front office and coaching staff.

They are feeling very, very good about the organization’s ability to develop hitting — and particularly power — in the majors and minors. They have every reason to, too, given that Mead went from floating in the ether to having a breakout year, including 17 home runs in less than four months. Players up and down the Nats’ major league roster are also tracking toward career highs in homers, if they aren’t there already. Which is all why it made perfect sense to trade from a position of strength (bats) to improve a glaring weakness (arms). (ESPN first reported the Mead-Early trade.)

Some more top-line details: Early is only 24 and will be under team control for another five years after this one (through 2031). Mead, 25, is controllable through 2030. Early has been on the injured list since July 1 with left elbow inflammation, which underscores the inherent risk of swapping a hitter for a pitcher who’s never thrown more than 104 innings at any level. But the Nats’ front office is intimately familiar with him, seeing that Paul Toboni, the team’s first-year president of baseball operations, was a key decision maker when Boston drafted Early in 2023, as was Devin Pearson, now one of Toboni’s assistant general managers in Washington. (Toboni has now done two deals with his former club.)

The deadline is Aug. 3, meaning the Nats could just be getting started. Shortstop CJ Abrams is generating real interest, according to multiple people familiar with his market, though it would take a massive return for the Nats to move him while hanging on the edge of the wild-race race. It wouldn’t require nearly as much for them to part with first baseman Luis García Jr. or starter Foster Griffin — though Griffin, an All Star with a 2.68 ERA, is in a higher tier than García, who would be a lefty platoon bat for a contender.

And if the Nationals can improve on their 53-52 record over the next week, they could very well seek bullpen help while weighing offers for the players above. If the Mead-Early trade revealed anything about their broader deadline approach, it is that it’s not necessarily a binary choice between buying or selling.

Early has allowed a ton of hard contact in 91⅔ innings this season. But he’s still managed a 3.44 ERA while mixing five to six pitches. Advanced metrics love his changeup. His extension, which measures the distance between the rubber and where a pitcher releases the ball, is well above average, a trait the Nats’ front office likes. And with the Red Sox, obvious needs lined up at the perfect time.

The Red Sox just ripped off a 15-game winning streak and needed more offense for their playoff push. The Nats, confident they can replicate the process that revived Mead’s career, leaped at the chance to bring in a high-upside pitcher they know well. The Red Sox have the pitching prospects to backfill Early’s spot. The Nats have a handful of intriguing infield prospects, including Brady House, who will join the team Sunday to replace Mead on the active roster (which The Athletic first reported). That’s the anatomy of a one-for-one trade of young big leaguers.

House will be the next test of just how well the Nats can coach up power hitting in the majors, which they’ve done with multiple players now by emphasizing pulling the right pitches in the air. A first-round pick in 2021, House started the year with the Nationals and struggled with contact and pitch selection. When he did connect, he hit the ball hard more often than not, resulting in seven homers in a limited sample. But he also struck out 50 times, nearly a third of this plate appearances, while working only 13 walks. Righties have chewed him up.

That’s not to say that House’s next two months should color the assessment of trading Mead for Early. House’s promotion doesn’t mean the Nationals necessarily view him as their third baseman of the future, especially given how they pulled Mead from obscurity to effectively replace House for a few months. But House, who just turned 23, is coming off an encouraging stretch in AAA. And if the major league staff can keep turning him in the right direction, Saturday’s deal will make even more sense.

entries.title: Trump’s Border Czar Says Vetting and Training for ICE Agents Is ‘Under Review’
entries.summary: The ICE agent who allegedly shot and killed a man in Maine should have had “an almost impossible time” passing vetting, Tom Homan said.
entries.content:
White House border czar Tom Homan said the vetting and training processes for Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents are “under review” after revelations that the agent who allegedly shot and killed an immigrant in Maine had been accused of domestic violence.

Homan said law enforcement agencies routinely review their training operations and ICE would evaluate “some additional training” as well as find out what may have gone wrong in vetting the ICE agent in Maine.

“Did we have that information? Did we not have that information?” Homan said Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union. “If that was factual, he would have an almost impossible time to pass vetting.”

ICE has not officially identified the agent who shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian man, in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13 — though The Associated Press and Boston Globe have reported that he is 37-year-old David Brouillette, who had previously served in the Army.

Brouillette’s family members and ex-wives have accused him of violent behavior and said he has a long history of psychiatric issues, several news outlets reported. If the accusations against Brouillette are true, Homan told CNN, he never should have cleared the vetting process.

“If this person had that type of history, it would have been a vetting issue, and it should have been brought to the attention of those who make those decisions,” Homan said.

The shooting in Maine happened less than a week after another fatal shooting in Houston where an ICE agent killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national.

Homan told CNN he did not “know specifically” the status of the officers involved in the shootings in Maine and Texas, but per ICE policy “they're usually put on administrative leave pending the investigation.”

Durán Guerrero and Salgado Araujo were both shot during vehicle stops. After the shootings, ICE temporarily paused most vehicle stops to review the enforcement tactic, but within a day, President Donald Trump directed the agency to resume traffic enforcement actions.

Homan said “changes have been made” to vehicle-stop procedures after acting ICE Director David Venturella gave officers new guidance on body-worn cameras. The Department of Homeland Security recently signed contracts for over $30 million to purchase the cameras. Venturella has also added training for officers, according to Homan.

“David Venturella sent an instruction out that he wants at least one body camera on those vehicle stops, so we have everything on video,” Homan told CNN.
